source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Nickles (1984, 1985, 1989) on discoverability
finding: Nickles splits justification in two. Consequential justification checks novel predictions. Generative justification shows a claim could have been reached from established results. Discoverability is the second kind.
numbers: No numbers. Newton's rule of deduction from the phenomena is the model case.
limits: Read through the SEP entry, a secondary source. Nickles' own texts not opened.
agent_relevance: S0 gate: an idea with a derivation path from known results earns earlier credit than one with only a vague story. Code can check that cited premises exist.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Schaffner (1993) on weak and strong evaluation
finding: Discovery procedures already contain appraisal. Weak evaluation gives reasons to take a hypothesis seriously enough to develop. Strong evaluation gives reasons to accept it as approximately true.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondary. The SEP entry does not describe a Schaffner 'logic of discovery' by name; it cites him for weak evaluation.
agent_relevance: Maps to a two-tier gate: a cheap 'worth developing' check at S0, a costly 'accept' check later. Do not spend strong-check budget on every idea.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Darden (1991, 2002, 2009) on schema instantiation
finding: Mechanism discovery runs in phases: generation, appraisal, revision. Each has strategies. Schema instantiation fills an abstract template. Protein synthesis started from 'reactant1 + reactant2 = product' and was then specified and modified.
numbers: No numbers. One worked example.
limits: SEP says the strategies are sufficient for discovery, not necessary, and only weakly normative. Darden's own papers not opened (PhilSci archive fetch was rejected).
agent_relevance: Operator idea: keep a library of abstract schemas, instantiate them, then repair. A template is a cheap way to make candidates that code can check.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Laudan (1980) on three contexts
finding: Laudan separates discovery proper, pursuit, and justification. Many methodologists fold pursuit into justification and keep two contexts.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: SEP does not spell out Laudan's arguments. Secondary only.
agent_relevance: Our pursuit decision (which idea gets budget) is the third context. It needs its own rule, not the rule for final acceptance.

source: Laudan (1980/1981) Why was the logic of discovery abandoned? (web-search commentary only)
finding: Commentary says Laudan rests his rejection of a logic of discovery on the 19th-century shift from generativism to consequentialism. In 1983 he conceded fallibilism does not rule it out. Critics say pursuit is not wholly outside discovery and justification, and that plausibility arguments link invention to appraisal.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Only snippets from a web search; the full text could not be downloaded. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Plausibility arguments are the bridge: a cheap pre-test of an idea can be rational without being proof. Supports a weak-appraisal step.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Hanson (1958, 1960) retroduction
finding: Hanson's schema: a surprising phenomenon appears. It would not be surprising if a hypothesis of type H held. So there is reason to elaborate type H. Kepler's Mars orbit is the example.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Lugg (1985) judges the Kepler reconstruction historically inadequate. Harman (1965): the schema is too permissive when many hypotheses explain the same data. Abduction does not say how an idea is first conceived.
agent_relevance: A surprise signal (check failed, attempts disagree) justifies searching for a hypothesis class. Ranking among candidates needs extra criteria.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Simon, Langley and Bradshaw (1981); Kulkarni and Simon (1988)
finding: Discovery as problem-space search. BACON detects regularities (a constant term, a linear relation) and re-derives Kepler's third law. KEKADA simulates the Krebs-cycle discovery with experiment-focused heuristics. Heuristics: means-ends analysis; split into sub-problems and start with the one with fewest unknowns.
numbers: Two worked re-discoveries (Kepler III, Krebs cycle). No error rates in the SEP text.
limits: Gillies (1996): a program cannot decide by itself which data are relevant or what form of law to seek. Re-discovery with a hand-picked representation is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Heuristic strategies as code-run operators. The choice of what to relate stays the hard part, so it is a model slot, not a program step.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising heuristic strategies and preliminary appraisal (sections 8.2, 8.3)
finding: Heuristics are open rules with no guarantee, but reasons can favour one over another (Gigerenzer; Nickles 2018 'tools to theory'). Preliminary appraisal applies field-specific criteria before rigorous testing, to decide whether a hypothesis merits further work.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Heuristics add systematic bias (Wimsatt 2007). Hey (2016) asks for general principles to evaluate heuristics.
agent_relevance: This is the S0 gate. Appraisal criteria are field-specific, so use task-type checks (can it run, does it fit held-out cases), not generic taste.

source: SEP 'Scientific Discovery' (Schickore) summarising Popper, Reichenbach, Whewell, Kuhn on the contexts
finding: The generate/assess split became a demarcation rule. Popper left conception outside logic. Reichenbach's own view was subtler. Kuhn treats discovery as an extended process that starts at an anomaly. Whewell: discovery has the happy thought, colligation, and verification.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: No maxims can be given which inevitably lead to discovery.
limits: Secondary.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: the trigger for new-idea search is an anomaly signal, not a timer.

source: SEP 'Scientific Method' on heuristics and the discovery-justification split
finding: Darden (1991) and Bechtel and Richardson (1993) treat science as problem solving with strategies to generate, evaluate and revise mechanistic explanations. Arabatzis (2006) argues the two contexts are inextricable. Nersessian (2008): no logic of discovery, but reasoned routes exist (analogy, imagery, thought experiments).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Secondary. No mention of pursuit or Peirce's economy of research in the text read.
agent_relevance: Generating and appraising are interleaved in real science; do not build a hard wall between them in the scaffold.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
finding: Blind expert review of ideas from NLP researchers versus an LLM ideation agent. AI ideas were rated more novel than human ideas.
numbers: 49 expert idea writers, 79 reviewers, 298 unique reviews, 7 topics, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty (1-10): Human 4.84 (SD 1.79), AI 5.64 (1.76), AI + human rerank 5.81 (1.66); p<0.01 with each review as a data point (Welch t, Bonferroni).
limits: Other metrics (feasibility, effectiveness, overall) mostly not significantly different. Ideas were style-normalised. Judged ideas, not executed work.
agent_relevance: A model can out-novel experts on paper. Paper novelty is not a safe signal for the pursuit decision (see the Ideation-Execution Gap).

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (reviewer reliability)
finding: Experts agree poorly on ideas. Split-half agreement on top and bottom 25% of ideas was low.
numbers: 56.1% inter-reviewer agreement on the balanced top/bottom task (50% is chance).
limits: Comparison with ICLR 2024 reviews is in the paper; exact ICLR figure not copied here.
agent_relevance: Appraisal of ideas is noisy even for experts. One judge, human or model, is a weak gate. Prefer running a cheap test.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (ranker and diversity)
finding: The agent generated a huge seed pool. Dedup at cosine similarity 0.8 left only about 5% non-duplicate ideas. An LLM ranker was only 71.4% accurate at accepted-versus-rejected paper pairs (Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot; GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%).
numbers: Dedup with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, threshold 0.8; k=10 retrieved papers in the prompt.
quote: failures of LLM self-evaluation and their lack of diversity in generation
limits: Authors name failure of LLM self-evaluation and low diversity as open problems. Ranker tested on paper accept/reject, a weak proxy for idea quality.
agent_relevance: Many samples from one model give few distinct ideas. Do dedup in code. The model's own ranking of ideas is barely useful.

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing a randomly assigned human or LLM idea. AI idea scores fell far more after execution than human idea scores. Rankings flipped on several metrics.
numbers: N=43 projects (19 human, 24 AI), 58 reviewers. Ideation, AI vs human: novelty 5.778 vs 4.912 (p=0.035), effectiveness 6.003 vs 4.833 (p=0.001). Execution overall: human 3.968 vs AI 3.406 (n.s., p=0.175). Drop gap (human minus AI) significant: novelty 1.039 (p=0.025), excitement 1.835 (p=0.001), effectiveness 1.827 (p=0.003), overall 1.348 (p=0.004).
limits: Per-idea execution differences not significant (N=43), so the flip is suggestive only. Modest sample, one field (NLP), one generator.
agent_relevance: Strongest warning for the pursuit gate: pre-execution appraisal over-rates LLM ideas. Spend budget by running, not by judged novelty (G8).

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap (ideation vs execution correlation)
finding: Pre-execution scores barely predict post-execution scores.
numbers: Appendix D: correlation weak in most cases; for AI ideas a moderately negative correlation on excitement.
limits: Small N; correlations noisy.
agent_relevance: Appraisal before running has little predictive value for LLM ideas. A pursuit rule should use cheap executed probes.

source: Zhou, Liu, Srivastava, Mei and Tan (2024) Hypothesis Generation with LLMs (HypoGeniC)
finding: Generate hypotheses from a few labelled examples, score by training accuracy, keep a bank, update with a UCB-style reward that trades exploitation against exploration. This is a computed pursuit rule: spend more tries on hypotheses that earn reward.
numbers: Accuracy gain over few-shot learning: +31.7% (synthetic shoe sales), +13.9% (deceptive reviews), +3.3% (headline popularity), +24.9% (tweet popularity). Beat supervised fine-tuning by 12.1% and 11.6% on two real sets. Bank updating helped on average by 0.7%, 5.8%, 8.1%, 7% on the four sets.
limits: Tweet result inflated because safety mode fired for some zero-shot LLMs. Gains are on classification sets, where a score exists.
agent_relevance: A bandit over candidate ideas with a code-computed reward is a working pursuit policy. It needs a checkable score.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: rediscovering unseen chemistry hypotheses
finding: Hypothesis discovery decomposed as background, retrieve inspiration papers, compose, rank. LLMs retrieved ground-truth inspiration papers far above chance.
limits: Measures retrieval of inspirations, not validity of the final hypothesis. Papers may be in training data. Chemistry only.
agent_relevance: Staged screening is a cheap preliminary appraisal that works at corpus scale. Fits a funnel for S0.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem (screening rounds)
finding: More screening rounds with a smaller window kept fewer papers and raised hit ratio.
numbers: Window of 15 keeping 3 for two rounds keeps 4% of corpus with hit ratio 83.7%; another setting keeps about 5% with 71.6%.
limits: Single benchmark; settings chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: Multi-round tournament screening beats one big ranking. Do the bookkeeping in code.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end pipeline: idea, novelty check against Semantic Scholar, code, experiments, paper, automated review. Cost under $15 per paper.
numbers: Automated reviewer: F1 0.57 vs 0.49 human, AUC 0.65 both, at threshold score 6 (weak accept); accuracy lower than the 73% NeurIPS 2021 human consistency figure.
limits: Authors list failure modes: ideas too hard to implement, wrong implementations hard to catch, hallucinated plots and facts, LaTeX failures.
agent_relevance: A search-based novelty check is a cheap pre-appraisal. Feasibility belongs in the gate.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist (implementation failures)
finding: The system proposes creative ideas but they are often too hard for it to implement, and it may implement them wrongly without notice. Authors advise manual checking of the code.
numbers: Tables 3-5 report ideas passing the novelty check vs ideas finishing experiments (exact counts not extracted this session).
limits: Per-model counts not read.
agent_relevance: Gate ideas on whether a run completes, and add an independent code check (G3).

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist
finding: Generate, debate, evolve with an Elo tournament as the pursuit selector. Elo rises with test-time compute. Experts preferred it over other frontier models.
numbers: 203 research goals for the Elo trend. 15 expert-curated goals vs Gemini 2.0, o1, o3-mini-high, DeepSeek R1 and the expert's best guess. Expert preference rank 2.36; novelty 3.64 and impact 3.09 out of 5 (11 goals).
limits: Elo is auto-evaluated, not ground truth; authors say so. Expert ratings subjective. Wet-lab validation for only a few hypotheses (AML, liver fibrosis).
agent_relevance: A pairwise tournament is a pursuit policy. The judge is a model, so it needs outside checks (G5, G8).

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench
finding: Benchmark for data-driven hypothesis search and verification. The best system solved about a quarter of tasks.
numbers: 264 real tasks in 6 domains plus 903 synthetic tasks. Best score 25% (hypothesis match score). Biology 0%, engineering 7%.
limits: Match score is LLM-judged. Replication of a dataset took up to 90 person-hours and 30% did not reproduce.
agent_relevance: Open-ended discovery is hard even for strong systems. Prefer tasks where a check exists.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: equation discovery with LLM programs
finding: A modern BACON-style loop: the LLM proposes equation skeletons from prior knowledge, data fits the parameters, evolutionary search keeps the best. Strong out-of-domain results.
numbers: Out-of-domain NMSE down to 0.0037 on one problem; baselines above 1. Ablations: dropping the prior-knowledge loop gave NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain and 1.81e-1 OOD; a changed representation gave 3.78e-1 and 3.75e-1.
limits: Four benchmarks built to block recitation. Fit is a first check; the OOD test is the real one.
agent_relevance: Held-out extrapolation as pass criterion (G3). Model priors plus code fitting beat either alone.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Towards an AI co-scientist (test-time compute)
finding: Elo of top hypotheses rose across iterations with no sign of saturation; newer reasoning models (o3-mini-high, DeepSeek R1) were competitive with much less compute.
numbers: Averaged over 203 research goals, bucketed by iteration; 15-goal subset consistent.
limits: Auto-evaluated Elo is the same family of judge that picks the winners, so the rise may partly reflect judge preference.
agent_relevance: More search budget helps only if the selector is trustworthy. Cap pursuit budget unless an external check confirms gains.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench (reflection with oracle)
finding: A reflection agent given an oracle hypothesis-match score retried up to 3 times. Even so, best performance peaked near 25%.
numbers: Max 3 trials; biology 0%, engineering 7%; easy workflow types (correlation analysis, data selection, summary statistics) did best.
limits: Oracle score is not available in real use.
agent_relevance: Retry only on a real external signal (G2). A model's own opinion will not replace the oracle.
